system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2116-06-11 01:57:00 to 2116-06-13 10:56:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and ongoing alcohol use, was admitted after a syncopal episode with a fall and head injury. He reported dizziness and a sensation of his implantable cardiac defibrillator firing, though device interrogation showed no recent activity. Initial evaluation revealed hypotension and lab findings consistent with dehydration, which improved with IV fluids. CT scans of the head and cervical spine showed no acute abnormalities, and a chest X-ray revealed a small right basilar opacity likely due to atelectasis. His symptoms were attributed to dehydration exacerbated by chronic alcohol use, Lasix therapy, and inappropriate use of nitroglycerin for device-pocket pain. His Lasix dose was adjusted to alternate between 20 mg and 40 mg daily, and he was counseled on hydration, avoiding alcohol, and not using nitroglycerin for non-cardiac pain. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up recommendations for primary care, liver monitoring, and device clinic evaluation for possible pocket revision.
problems: Unspecified disorder of kidney and ureter
Automatic implantable cardiac defibrillator in situ

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with right lower lobe pulmonary embolism
diagnosed ___, on Lovenox, atrial fibrillation with systolic heart failure
post-AICD placement, had acute onset chest pain and vomiting x4 hours.

COMPARISON:  CTA chest from ___ and CT abdomen/pelvis from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Helical MDCT images were acquired through the chest before and
after the uneventful administration of 130 cc of intravenous Omnipaque.  5-,
2.5-, and 1.25-mm axial, 5-mm coronal and sagittal, and 3-mm bilateral oblique
multiplanar reformats were generated.  Abdominal CT was subsequently ordered,
and the patient was brought back for injection of additional 70 cc of
intravenous Omnipaque.  Helical MDCT images were acquired through the abdomen
and pelvis, and 5-mm axial, coronal, and sagittal multiplanar reformats were
generated.

FINDINGS:

CHEST:  There is no acute main, branch, lobar, or segmental pulmonary embolus.
Prior acute subsegmental embolus in the right lower lobe has resolved. 
Concomitant evolution of the associated pulmonary infarct, now with a
wedge-shaped area of subpleural scarring and dystrophic calcification.  Right
pleural effusion has cleared.  Chronic eccentric thrombus in the posterior
basal segment of the left lower lobe (3:48), stable over multiple
examinations.  

No pulmonary masses or focal consoldiation.  Mild retained secretions in the
trachea.  Note is made of a tracheal diverticulum at the carina.  Central
airways are patent to subsegmental levels.

Right ventricular pacemaker/AICD lead courses in expected position.  Mild
cardiomegaly persists, with trace physiologic pericardial fluid.

Note is made of mediastinal lipomatosis.  Axillary, hilar, and mediastinal
lymph nodes are not pathologically enlarged.

ABDOMEN:  There is diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver, with stable 6-mm
hypodensity in segment VII.  Gallbladder is partially collapsed.  The pancreas
is normal.  No intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilation.  The spleen is
normal in size.

The adrenals are normal.  Kidneys enhance and excrete contrast promptly and
symmetrically, without masses or hydronephrosis.

The stomach and small bowel are normal.

PELVIS:  The colon and rectum are normal.  Bladder is distended with urine,
with bilateral ureteral jets visualized.  Prostate and seminal vesicles are
prominent.  There is no free intraperitoneal fluid or air.

Multiple small retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymph nodes are present.

Chronic mild anterior compression deformity of T12, with 20% loss of anterior
height.Unchanged grade 1 retrolisthesis of L5-S1, with endplate sclerosis and
intervertebral vacuum disc phenomenon.  

IMPRESSION:

1.  No acute PE.  Resolved right lower lobe PE with evolving infarct.  Chronic
left lower lobe PE.

2.  Mild cardiomegaly.

3.  Fatty liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU. You came in with chest pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… chest pain started last night around 8:30. I took five nitroglycerin pills, but it didn’t help. I’ve been throwing up all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how much have you been drinking lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Usually a gallon a day… but this time, only about half a pint. Haven’t eaten much either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your heart rate is very high—around 140. We think this might be due to your heart rhythm, possibly atrial fibrillation or flutter, made worse by not eating or drinking enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? My heart’s been acting up before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your history of heart failure. But we’re monitoring you closely. We gave you fluids and some medication to help slow your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel sweaty and weak. Is the chest pain from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your troponin—it’s normal, so no active heart attack. But your EKG shows changes that suggest your heart isn’t getting enough oxygen, likely because it’s beating too fast. We call that demand ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… so fixing the rhythm might help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Cardiology is involved. We may need to do a cardioversion—a procedure to reset your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be asleep for it. Very safe. We’ll let you know when it’s scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your labs show low magnesium and potassium. We’re giving replacements through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my heart’s racing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Low levels like this, plus dehydration and alcohol use, can trigger arrhythmias. Your liver enzymes are also elevated, which we think is from drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stomach ulcers before. Could that be why I’m vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But your CT scan of the abdomen was normal. No signs of bleeding or blockage. We’ll keep giving anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan to rule out a blood clot in your lungs. Good news—it’s negative. No pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had one before. I’m supposed to be on blood thinners, but I forget sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Because of your history, staying on anticoagulants helps prevent clots. But since you’ve had trouble with compliance, cardioversion might help avoid long-term blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart went into atrial flutter earlier. We gave IV verapamil, which helped briefly. Cardiology still recommends cardioversion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So when will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow, likely around noon. We want to make sure you’re stable and your electrolytes are corrected first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re scheduling your cardioversion for noon today. You’ll be under sedation, and we’ll deliver a small shock to reset your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doc. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re awake. The cardioversion was successful. You’re now in normal sinus rhythm. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better… chest pain’s gone. Heart feels calmer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your heart rate is down to 80 and regular. We’ll keep monitoring you. You’ll now be on oral verapamil to help maintain this rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a new pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It helps control your heart rate. We’re also continuing your other heart meds—metoprolol, losartan, aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your liver tests again—they’re improving. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working toward that. But you still have some nausea. We need you to keep fluids down before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up again… just a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you more anti-nausea medication. It’s common after all this stress on your body. We’ll keep managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable, you’re keeping food down, and your heart rhythm is holding. We’re planning to discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your new verapamil daily. Keep taking your other meds. Stop drinking alcohol completely—it’s critical for your heart and liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I’ve got to make a change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And follow up with your primary doctor and cardiologist. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re also connecting you with social work—they can help with housing and support for stopping drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand. Take my pills, no alcohol, follow up, and watch my weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of heavy alcohol use, was admitted for vomiting and chest pain with tachycardia. His symptoms began after minimal oral intake and reduced alcohol consumption, leading to volume depletion and possible early withdrawal. Initial evaluation revealed a rapid heart rate due to atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, later transitioning to atrial flutter. He underwent successful elective cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm and was started on verapamil for rate control. Chest pain was attributed to demand ischemia from tachycardia, with no evidence of acute infarction. Elevated liver enzymes were consistent with alcohol use and improved during the stay. Nausea and vomiting, possibly related to his history of peptic ulcer disease, resolved with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to discontinue alcohol, adhere to new and existing cardiac medications, monitor weight, and follow up with primary and specialty care. Social work was engaged to assist with housing and substance use support.
